ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval for the eMotion study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Psychology and Sports Science at the University of Münster, under registration number 2021-81-AM.

Inclusion criteria for the eMotion study required that participants (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) were fluent in German, (c) were in a committed romantic relationship for a minimum of six months, (d) had both partners in the relationship be willing to participate, and (e) had at least one partner own an Android smartphone.
Most participants had completed secondary education or higher (87.7%), with 54.1% holding a university degree.
Participants were employed either full-time (39.2%) or part-time (41.5%) and had been in their romantic relationship for an average of 8.1 years (SD = 7.7, range = 6 months -49 years).
Prompts were randomized independently for each participant and each day.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Effects of Smartphone Use Purposes on Psychological Well-being
table.research_questions:
Given that past research on the relationship between smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being has focused on self-reported data, we find it difficult to make an informed decision about which associations to expect when looking at traced smartphone use data. However, going by findings that appear consistent between our prior studies and past research, we prudently hypothesize the following:

First, at a within-person level, we expect that longer smartphone use for active social purposes will be associated with higher self-reported stress (H1). Further, we expect that longer smartphone use for passive social purposes will be associated with higher negative affect (H2).

Next, at a between-person level, we expect that participants with longer active social smartphone use will have higher positive affect and higher stress compared to participants with shorter active social smartphone use (H3a, H3b). Finally, we expect that participants with longer passive social smartphone use will have higher negative affect and higher stress compared to participants with shorter passive social use (H4a, H4b).

We will investigate the relationships between the remaining smartphone use purposes (i.e., news consumption, entertainment, practical) and psychological well-being in an exploratory manner.
table.study_type: Observational Study - Data is collected from study subjects that are not randomly assigned to a treatment. This includes surveys, “natural experiments,” and regression discontinuity designs.
table.blinding: No blinding is involved in this study.
table.study_design_overview: Data is collected as part of a larger experience-sampling project (the “eMotion” study) at the University of Witten/Herdecke. The eMotion study combines ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and mobile sensing to assess the impact of smartphones on the physiological and psychological well-being of romantic couples. The eMotion study begins with a baseline survey in which participants report their demographic information and complete several trait measures. Next, for a period of 10 days, participants and their romantic partners are simultaneously prompted up to six times per day. The first five prompts contain the same survey with several state measures. The sixth prompt is administered at the end of the day and contains a shorter, evening survey, along with questions about participants’ entire day. Throughout the 10-day study period, mobile sensing data (e.g., app usage log, phone sensor data, etc.) is automatically obtained from the smartphones of participants who provide additional consent to the procedure. At the end of the study period, participants complete a final survey with additional trait measures. Participants are eligible to receive up to 118 EUR as compensation, contingent on which parts of the study they took part in, and how many of the daily questionnaires were completed. As additional compensation, participants may also indicate whether to receive individualized feedback, which is then directly sent to their email.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to analysis of the data
table.existing_data_explanation:
Presently, N = 506 participants (N = 253 couples) have taken part in the eMotion study. Subsets of data from the eMotion study have previously been examined as part of the following studies:

“Within-person associations between objectively measured pre-bedtime smartphone usage and sleep” (https://osf.io/d3sjm)

“Exploring the potential of mobile sensing for measuring time apent together in couples” (https://osf.io/hbrqn)

“The moderation of one’s own phubbing behavior on the association between perceived phubbing and threats to fundamental needs” (https://osf.io/dzvyj)

However, we note that there is no overlap between the present study and those listed above with regards to research question(s), focal variables, hypotheses, and planned analyses.

Next, we note that sub-samples of the mobile sensing data have been used to test pre-processing scripts which aim to extract various features (e.g., screen time, app usage, etc.) from the trace data. However, no statistical analyses have currently been conducted on the resulting pre-processed data.
table.data_collection_procedures: Participants who registered for the eMotion study were first contacted by a team of recruiters for a briefing round in which the purpose and procedure of the study are explained. Following this, recruiters entered essential information (e.g., couple ID, starting date, etc.) from consenting participants into the administrative portal of formR, through which most aspects of the EMA procedure have been automated. Links to the EMA prompts were sent to participants via SMS through the Massenversand service. Participants received six daily prompts between 09:30 and 21:00 over the course of 10 days. Each prompt was randomly scheduled within one of six 69-minute intervals throughout the day (e.g., notification 1 between 09:30 and 10:39, notification 2 between 11:30 and 12:39, etc.). A 51-minute gap was maintained between these six intervals to accommodate a 30-minute window for participants to open the survey, a 10-minute completion time, and a potential 11-minute CRON job delay for sending prompts. The sixth prompt (i.e., the final prompt of the day) was sent at 21:30 every evening. Participants were given 60 minutes to open this evening questionnaire and 10 minutes to complete it. During the briefing round, participants who consented to the mobile sensing portion of the study were asked to install the movisensXS app on their smartphones, which allowed smartphone trace data to be automatically obtained throughout the study. All obtained data was stored on university-protected servers.
table.sample_size:
The present study will use data from all participants with Android smartphones who have consented to the mobile sensing procedure. Mobile sensing data is thus available from N = 395 participants, nested in couples.

Given that data from the eMotion study is dyadic in nature, it is likely that intradyadic processes may influence day-to-day changes in participants’ psychological well-being, resulting in interdependencies that violate most assumptions of ordinary analytic strategies. Due to unforeseen quirks in the data collection process (e.g., the mobile sensing platform not working on certain types of smartphones), dyadic app event log data (i.e., where both members of a dyad consented to the mobile sensing procedure) are available for N = 139 couples (N = 278 participants) only. For the remaining participants (N = 117), only single data is available. We thus plan to split the couple members (N = 278) into two data subsets and randomly assign the singles (N = 117) to either subset, ensuring participant demographic characteristics are comparable between the two subsets. We will then run our planned analyses in each data subset. This allows us to leverage the complete data set to investigate our hypotheses, while taking the interdependencies of the dyadic data into account.
table.sample_size_rationale: Sample size was determined based on availability of resources.
table.stopping_rule: Data collection for the eMotion study was stopped on 5 May 2025.
table.measured_variables:
We plan to use the following variables from the eMotion study:

Emotions
-----
Measured using a series of items adapted from Kuppens (2013) and Sonnentag et al. (2008). Participants reported the extent to which they felt the following emotions at the time of measurement: happiness, relaxation, sadness, irritation, worry, depression, and exhaustion. Participants reported their answers on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much) scale, with higher scores indicating higher prevalence of each specific emotion. Emotions were measured during the five daily prompts and during the final end-of-day prompt. We will use all measured emotion data (all prompts, all days) in our planned analyses.

Self-reported stress
-----
Measured using the Stress Overload Scale (SOS; Amirkhan, 2011). The SOS consists of 5 items which assessed the extent to which participants felt overwhelmed by daily demands or stressors at the time of measurement (e.g., “to what extent did you feel overwhelmed by your duties today?”). The SOS was scored on a 1 (not at all) to 7 (very much) scale, with higher scores indicating higher self-reported stress. Self-reported stress was measured during the final end-of-day prompt. We will use all self-reported stress data in our planned analyses.

App event logs
-----
Measured using the movisensXS mobile sensing platform. The movisensXS platform automatically tracked which smartphone apps were used by participants throughout the 10-day study period. Each log is stored in the following format: [time],[class],[event], where [time] is the amount of time that has elapsed since the movisensXS app began recording trace data (in epoch time, e.g., “51432”), [class] represents the type of event that is logged (e.g., App), and [event] identifies the smartphone app that was used (e.g., com.whatsapp/.MainActivity).

Based on the logged event data, participants’ smartphone app use was categorized into one of 26 categories listed in Schoedel et al. (2022). These are: audio entertainment, career, communication, creativity, dating, finance, food, gaming, health, internet, knowledge, news, orientation, photo, reading, security, settings, shopping, social media, spirituality, system, time, tools, transportation, visual entertainment, and weather. Please see Schoedel et al. (2022) for a more detailed description of each of the 26 smartphone app categories.
table.indices:
The following indices will be calculated:

Positive affect
-----
All happiness and relaxation scores (prompts 1-6) will be averaged per day to obtain an indicator of daily positive affect.

Negative affect
-----
All sadness, irritation, worry, depression, and exhaustion scores (prompts 1-6) will be averaged per day to obtain an indicator of daily negative affect.

Smartphone use purposes
-----
To obtain these indices, a second categorization step will first be applied on the app use categories that have been identified from the app event logs (see ‘App use’ under ‘Measured variables’). In this second categorization step, we plan to sort each identified app category into one of the five smartphone use purposes utilized in the present study. The categorization procedure will use the following guideline, which matches definitions for each app category in Schoedel et al. (2022) with the definitions for each app use purpose in our study:
> Active social use: communication; dating.
> Passive social use: social media.
> News consumption: news.
> Entertainment: audio entertainment; creativity; gaming; photo; reading; visual entertainment.
> Practical use: career; finance; food; health; knowledge; orientation; security; shopping; spirituality; time; tools; transportation; weather.

We chose to exclude the ‘internet’ app category from the categorization guideline above, as the use of internet apps can fulfill multiple purposes (Schoedel et al., 2022), which cannot be distinguished based on information in each participants’ app event logs. Further, based on suggestions in Parry and Toth (2024), we excluded the ’settings’ and ‘system’ app categories, as their typical use cases (e.g., changing screen brightness, accessing a smartphone’s home screen or list of apps) do not fit any of our five app use categories.

Following this second categorization step, we will extract the daily duration of each smartphone use purpose. This represents the total time a participants’ smartphone was used for a given purpose each day (e.g., “15 minutes of active social use”, 60 minutes of passive social use”, etc.).

Total screen time
------
To obtain this index, we will aggregate the duration of each participants’ app use sessions per day, which are demarcated by ‘screen on’ and ‘screen off’ events in participants’ respective app event logs. Excluding potential unrealistically long app usage sessions, this index is taken to represent the total time a participant interacted with their smartphone in a day.
table.statistical_tests:
To investigate our hypotheses, we plan to conduct several multi-level models:

Basic model
-----
psychological well-being ~ day + duration smartphone use purpose + total screen time

Based on our hypotheses, we thus plan on running the following models:

Positive affect
-----
positive affect ~ day + duration active social use + total screen time
> Hypothesis (between-person): participants with longer active social smartphone use report higher positive affect compared to participants with shorter active social use (H3a)

Negative affect
-----
negative affect ~ day + duration passive social use + total screen time
> Hypothesis (within-person): longer passive social smartphone use is associated with higher negative affect at the day level (H2)
> Hypothesis (between-person): participants with longer passive social smartphone use report higher negative affect compared to participants with shorter passive social use (H4a)

Self-reported stress
-----
self-reported stress ~ day + duration active social use + total screen time
> Hypothesis (within-person): longer active social smartphone use is associated with higher self-reported stress at the day-level (H1)
> Hypothesis (between-person): participants with longer active social smartphone use report higher self-reported tress compared to participants with shorter active social use (H3b)

self-reported stress ~ day + duration passive social use + total screen time
> Hypothesis (between-person): participants with longer passive social smartphone use report higher self-reported stress compared to participants with shorter passive social use (H4b)

In each of the above models, we plan to include the within- (i.e., day-to-day changes) and between-person (i.e., overall tendencies) effects for smartphone use purpose. As participants’ app use may vary from day to day, we plan to specify random intercepts and random slopes for the within-person effects of smartphone use purpose. If the initial multi-level models fail to converge, the random-effects structure will be simplified to only allow random intercepts per participant.
table.transformations: Smartphone use purpose will first be centered by subtracting within-person means. Next, participant-level means will be calculated by averaging smartphone use purpose duration for all days. These participant-level means are then centered by subtracting the grand mean.
table.inference_criteria: To interpret the results of each of our statistical models, we will use the standard inference criterion of α = 0.05. However, given that our planned analyses will be conducted in two data subsets, we will not draw inference from individual models but rather examine the pattern of findings that emerges from the two data subsets.
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
We will apply the following exclusion criteria:
> We will exclude participants with <40% EMA completion. This helps ensure that our planned multiple imputation procedure (see ‘Missing data’) will still yield reliable estimates.
> We will exclude participant days if unrealistically long gaps in the logging data, unrealistically long (app) use sessions, logging errors (e.g., missing ‘screen on’ or ‘screen off’ events), etc. will result in more than 10 minutes of missing recordings.
table.missing_data_handling: Following data exclusion, missing information for the measured variables will be handled through a bootstrapped multiple imputation procedure prior to creating our indices. We will first conduct a test to examine the pattern of missingness in the data and apply multiple imputation when the data is deemed missing completely at random (MCAR) or missing at random (MAR). When patterns of missing data are not MCAR, listwise deletion will be applied.
table.exploratory_analyses: We plan to exploratorily investigate the relationships between the remaining smartphone use purposes (i.e., news consumption, entertainment, practical) and psychological well-being through use of the basic statistical model we have previously specified.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("ps > .30", "ps > .05", "ps > .10", 
"ps > .08", "ps > .05", "ps > .13"), Text = c("Between-person passive social use was not significantly associated with positive affect, negative affect, or perceived stress in either subset (all ps > .30; Table S2).", 
"Within-person passive social use was likewise not significantly associated with any psychological well-being outcome in either subset (all ps > .05; Table S2).", 
"Within-person news consumption was not significantly associated with any psychological well-being outcome in either subset (all ps > .10; Table S3).", 
"Between-person entertainment use was not significantly associated with positive affect, negative affect, or perceived stress in either subset (all ps > .08; Table S4).", 
"Between-person practical use was not significantly associated with positive affect, negative affect, or perceived stress in either subset (all ps > .05; Table S5).", 
"Within-person practical use was not significantly associated with any psychological well-being outcome in either subset (all ps > .13; Table S5)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1811 columns across 2 data files.
#### Issues Identified

236 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

347 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **57 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 2 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethical approval for the eMotion study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Psychology and Sports Science at the University of Münster, under registration number 2021-81-AM.
live_data_statements: Inclusion criteria for the eMotion study required that participants (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) were fluent in German, (c) were in a committed romantic relationship for a minimum of six months, (d) had both partners in the relationship be willing to participate, and (e) had at least one partner own an Android smartphone.
Most participants had completed secondary education or higher (87.7%), with 54.1% holding a university degree.
Participants were employed either full-time (39.2%) or part-time (41.5%) and had been in their romantic relationship for an average of 8.1 years (SD = 7.7, range = 6 months -49 years).
Prompts were randomized independently for each participant and each day.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "tmh20260809_analysis.R", "Runs after" = "—", 
    Basis = "numeric"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 2 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `ba_data_cleaned.sav`, `5_emotion_onerowperday_combined.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "tmh20260809_analysis.R", Outcome = "errored", 
    Detail = "runtime", "Time (s)" = 6.6), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "tmh20260809_analysis.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, 
    "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

#### SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (`.sav`/`.por`) is present but **no SPSS syntax file (`.sps`) was found**, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in **jamovi** (`.omv`) or **JASP** (`.jasp`) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

text.text: Research on smartphone use and psychological well-being has yielded ambivalent and generally small effects.

Three methodological limitations contribute to this inconsistency: studies typically capture smartphone use through aggregate measures such as screen time, rely on self-reported estimates that are systematically biased, and focus predominantly on betweenperson differences while neglecting within-person dynamics.
The present study addresses these limitations by examining the between-and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being.

Using device logged app use data from a 10-day ecological momentary assessment study of romantic couples (N = 342 individuals), we examined five smartphone use purposes -active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, and practical use -in relation to positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress.
Analyses were replicated across two subsets to circumvent the dyadic structure of the data, and as an internal robustness check.
Across both subsets, associations between digitally traced use purposes and well-being were overall modest and largely inconsistent.
The only robust finding across subsets was a within-person association suggesting that days of higher than typical active social use were associated with lower positive affect.
Notably, passive social use, which is among the strongest negative predictors of well-being in self-report studies, showed no reliable association under device logged measurement.

Overall, these findings suggest that the psychological consequences of actual smartphone use behavior are more limited and more context-dependent than self-report studies imply, underscoring the importance of measurement methods in research on digital technology and well-being.
Smartphones have become deeply embedded in our daily lives (Fortunati, 2023; Roehrick et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Smartphones have become deeply embedded in our daily lives <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Fortunati, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Roehrick et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: For many, smartphones mediate core everyday activities, including communication, access to information, entertainment, and navigation, with use extending across waking hours, from the morning alarm to the final moments before sleep (Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021).
text.formatted: For many, smartphones mediate core everyday activities, including communication, access to information, entertainment, and navigation, with use extending across waking hours, from the morning alarm to the final moments before sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Heitmayer & Lahlou, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Against this backdrop, public concern about the psychological consequences of widespread smartphone use has grown considerably (Horwood & Anglim, 2019; van Velthoven et al., 2018), to the extent that "digital detox" interventions have been proposed to reduce the potential harm of our reliance on smartphones (Radtke et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Against this backdrop, public concern about the psychological consequences of widespread smartphone use has grown considerably <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Horwood & Anglim, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">van Velthoven et al., 2018)</ref>, to the extent that "digital detox" interventions have been proposed to reduce the potential harm of our reliance on smartphones <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Radtke et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, despite a substantial body of existing research, empirical evidence on the association between smartphone use and psychological well-being remains equivocal: effect sizes are typically small, findings are inconsistent across studies, and conclusions about the psychological consequences of daily smartphone use range from mildly harmful to essentially negligible (Johannes et al., 2021; Kushlev & Leitao, 2020).
text.formatted: Yet, despite a substantial body of existing research, empirical evidence on the association between smartphone use and psychological well-being remains equivocal: effect sizes are typically small, findings are inconsistent across studies, and conclusions about the psychological consequences of daily smartphone use range from mildly harmful to essentially negligible <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Johannes et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kushlev & Leitao, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, we argue that this drawback is partly a product of how smartphone use has been conceptualized and measured.

In addressing this shortcoming, we aim to not only advance our understanding of the relationship between smartphone use and well-being, but also to ensure that public concern and intervention efforts are based on reliable evidence.
An important limitation in existing literature is that smartphone use behavior has generally been studied using screen time as a proxy.
However, screen time may not accurately reflect individuals' actual smartphone use behavior, as this behavior is highly heterogeneous (Kaye et al., 2020; Toth et al., 2025).
text.formatted: However, screen time may not accurately reflect individuals' actual smartphone use behavior, as this behavior is highly heterogeneous <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kaye et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Toth et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, studies have noted considerable diversity in individuals' smartphone use behavior, both across individuals and within individuals over time (Griffioen et al., 2021; Twenge & Farley, 2021; Zhao et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Consistent with this, studies have noted considerable diversity in individuals' smartphone use behavior, both across individuals and within individuals over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Griffioen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Twenge & Farley, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Zhao et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Given this diversity, what individuals use their smartphones for may be more psychologically consequential than how long they use their smartphones overall (Nawaz, 2024; Schenkel et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Given this diversity, what individuals use their smartphones for may be more psychologically consequential than how long they use their smartphones overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Nawaz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Schenkel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Zhao et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing on van Deursen and colleagues' (2015) framework of smartphone use motivations, individuals use smartphones to fulfill qualitatively distinct needs (cf. uses and gratifications theory; Leung & Wei, 2000; Ruggiero, 2000), namely contentrelated needs (e.g., seeking and processing information), process-related needs (e.g., enjoyment, distraction, and recovery), and social needs (e.g., connection and belonging).
text.formatted: Drawing on van Deursen and colleagues' (2015) framework of smartphone use motivations, individuals use smartphones to fulfill qualitatively distinct needs (cf. uses and gratifications theory; <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Leung & Wei, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Ruggiero, 2000)</ref>, namely contentrelated needs (e.g., seeking and processing information), process-related needs (e.g., enjoyment, distraction, and recovery), and social needs (e.g., connection and belonging).

text.text: Notably, van Deursen and colleagues' framework does not assume that smartphone use is inherently detrimental or beneficial.
Rather, the framework suggests that the psychological consequences of smartphone use depend on the functions it serves.
In line with this framework, the present study focuses on five smartphone use purposes that map onto conceptually distinct functional domains.

These are active social use (e.g., calling, messaging, posting), passive social use (e.g., scrolling through social media feeds without active engagement; cf. 'zombie-scrolling', Yousef et al., 2025), news consumption, entertainment (e.g., watching videos, gaming, listening to music), and practical use (e.g., navigation, scheduling, task management).
text.formatted: These are active social use (e.g., calling, messaging, posting), passive social use (e.g., scrolling through social media feeds without active engagement; cf. 'zombie-scrolling', <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Yousef et al., 2025)</ref>, news consumption, entertainment (e.g., watching videos, gaming, listening to music), and practical use (e.g., navigation, scheduling, task management).

text.text: Each use purpose reflects a different combination of content, process, and social gratifications, and may therefore relate differently to well-being: First, active social use may support psychological well-being through the fulfilment of social needs (Bian & Leung, 2015; Kroencke et al., 2023), while passive social use may limit reciprocal social exchange and invite upward social comparison, leading to higher negative affect and lower overall well-being (Meier & Krause, 2023; Verduyn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Each use purpose reflects a different combination of content, process, and social gratifications, and may therefore relate differently to well-being: First, active social use may support psychological well-being through the fulfilment of social needs <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bian & Leung, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Kroencke et al., 2023)</ref>, while passive social use may limit reciprocal social exchange and invite upward social comparison, leading to higher negative affect and lower overall well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Meier & Krause, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verduyn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction between active and passive social use is also reflected in the interaction level of Meier and Reinecke's (2021) taxonomy of computer-mediated communication, where active use involves reciprocal exchange between communication partners, while passive use reflects one-way, non-interactive consumption.

text.text: Next, news consumption may either uplift or undermine well-being depending on the valence, utility, and personal relevance of the content viewed (Boukes & Vliegenthart, 2017; de Hoog & Verboon, 2020; Kelly & Sharot, 2021).

text.text: Meanwhile, entertainment use may promote well-being by facilitating recovery experiences such as psychological detachment, mastery, relaxation, and control (Koçak et al., 2024; Sonnentag et al., 2022; Zhang & Zhu, 2025).
text.formatted: Meanwhile, entertainment use may promote well-being by facilitating recovery experiences such as psychological detachment, mastery, relaxation, and control <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Koçak et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Sonnentag et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Zhang & Zhu, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, practical use may support well-being by increasing the efficiency of everyday tasks and reducing associated cognitive load (Bishnoi & Mirhoseini, 2025; Eisenstadt et al., 2021; Stiglbauer et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Finally, practical use may support well-being by increasing the efficiency of everyday tasks and reducing associated cognitive load <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bishnoi & Mirhoseini, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Eisenstadt et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Stiglbauer et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Distinguishing between smartphone use purposes thus offers a shift beyond aggregate measures of smartphone use behavior toward a more functionally grounded understanding of how smartphone use may relate to psychological well-being.
A second limitation in existing work concerns how smartphone use is measured.
Currently, most studies linking smartphone use to psychological well-being have relied on selfreported estimates of screen time (Ellis, 2019; Kaye et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Currently, most studies linking smartphone use to psychological well-being have relied on selfreported estimates of screen time <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ellis, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kaye et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, self-reported estimates of smartphone use are not only imprecise but are also prone to being systematically biased.

Individuals often overestimate their smartphone use, and these perceptual biases may themselves be associated with well-being in ways that inflate any observed associations (Coyne et al., 2023; Parry et al., 2021; Sewall & Parry, 2021; Tkaczyk et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Individuals often overestimate their smartphone use, and these perceptual biases may themselves be associated with well-being in ways that inflate any observed associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Coyne et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Parry et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sewall & Parry, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Tkaczyk et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, when both smartphone use and psychological well-being are measured through self-report, shared method variance may yield spurious associations that mask the genuine relationship between the two variables (Orben & Przybylski, 2019; Podsakoff et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Consequently, when both smartphone use and psychological well-being are measured through self-report, shared method variance may yield spurious associations that mask the genuine relationship between the two variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Orben & Przybylski, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Podsakoff et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this, studies relying on self-reported data tend to report more consistent and more pronounced negative associations between smartphone use and well-being, whereas studies using digitally traced data typically yield smaller, less consistent, and more equivocal effects (Johannes et al., 2021; Kushlev & Leitao, 2020).
text.formatted: In line with this, studies relying on self-reported data tend to report more consistent and more pronounced negative associations between smartphone use and well-being, whereas studies using digitally traced data typically yield smaller, less consistent, and more equivocal effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Johannes et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kushlev & Leitao, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: For example, studies have linked higher self-reported smartphone use to elevated depression, anxiety, and stress in different populations, as well as to lower life satisfaction and overall well-being (Fortes et al., 2021; Kil et al., 2021; Ong et al., 2024; Studer et al., 2022; Vahedi & Saiphoo, 2018).

text.text: In contrast, studies have only found modest, positive associations between digitally traced smartphone use and daily well-being, alongside negative between-person associations reflecting lower well-being among more frequent users (große Deters & Schoedel, 2024; Marciano et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In contrast, studies have only found modest, positive associations between digitally traced smartphone use and daily well-being, alongside negative between-person associations reflecting lower well-being among more frequent users <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(große Deters & Schoedel, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Marciano et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the use of digitally traced smartphone data offers an important corrective: it enables a more objective assessment of whether and how smartphone use behavior, rather than smartphone use perceptions, relates to psychological well-being.
The final limitation of existing research concerns the level of analysis at which associations are estimated.
Smartphone use varies both between individuals, who differ in how much and for what purpose they typically use their phones, and within individuals, whose smartphone use fluctuates from day to day.
Studies have often estimated associations that either confound these two sources of variation or are exclusively at the between-person level.

However, the distinction between these two levels is important (Marciano et al., 2022; Meier & Reinecke, 2021): between-person associations indicate whether individuals who habitually use their smartphone in specific ways differ in their typical well-being, which is a question underlying much of the public discourse surrounding smartphone use (Horwood & Anglim, 2019; Vahedi & Saiphoo, 2018; Van Velthoven et al., 2018).
text.formatted: However, the distinction between these two levels is important <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Marciano et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Meier & Reinecke, 2021)</ref>: between-person associations indicate whether individuals who habitually use their smartphone in specific ways differ in their typical well-being, which is a question underlying much of the public discourse surrounding smartphone use <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Horwood & Anglim, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Vahedi & Saiphoo, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Velthoven et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, between-person associations are susceptible to the influence of stable individual characteristics, including personality, social circumstances, and occupational demands, which are known to simultaneously predict well-being (Anglim et al., 2020; Huppert, 2009).
text.formatted: However, between-person associations are susceptible to the influence of stable individual characteristics, including personality, social circumstances, and occupational demands, which are known to simultaneously predict well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Huppert, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, withinperson associations hold the individual constant and capture how deviations from an individual's own typical behavior correspond to changes in their well-being.
Crucially, between-and within-person estimates do not need to converge.
Instead, they may differ in magnitude and occasionally in direction (Curran & Bauer, 2011; Valkenburg et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Instead, they may differ in magnitude and occasionally in direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Curran & Bauer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Valkenburg et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Estimating both levels simultaneously is therefore critical to understanding whether the associations between smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being reflect enduring individual differences, short-term fluctuations, or both.
The present study addresses the above limitations by examining the between-and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being.

This study builds directly on prior work in which the same research question was examined using self-reported smartphone use data, yielding evidence that different smartphone use purposes were distinctly associated with well-being, with passive social use being consistently linked to lower well-being overall (Adiasto et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This study builds directly on prior work in which the same research question was examined using self-reported smartphone use data, yielding evidence that different smartphone use purposes were distinctly associated with well-being, with passive social use being consistently linked to lower well-being overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We based our current hypotheses on the findings of this previous study, refraining from making predictions when prior evidence was absent or inconsistent.

Crucially, we replaced selfreported estimates of smartphone use with passively collected digital trace data, to provide a more objective test of whether the previously found associations are driven by actual smartphone use behavior.

Given the multidimensional nature of psychological well-being (Hernandez et al., 2018; Ryff & Keyes, 1995), we examined three established indicators in the present study, namely positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress.
text.formatted: Given the multidimensional nature of psychological well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Hernandez et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ryff & Keyes, 1995)</ref>, we examined three established indicators in the present study, namely positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress.

text.text: Based on the above, we hypothesized that digitally traced active social use would be positively associated with positive affect at a between-person level.
Concurrently, we expected that active social use would be positively associated with stress at the between-and within-person levels.
Next, we hypothesized that digitally traced passive social use would be associated with lower well-being at the between-person level, but not at the within-person level.
Associations between the remaining use purposes (i.e., news consumption, entertainment, practical use) and well-being were examined exploratorily.
Data used in the present study were obtained from the 'eMotion' study: a large-scale ecological momentary assessment (EMA) of the impact of smartphone use on lives of romantic couples.
Hypotheses and statistical analyses were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/hd3yq) repository.
text.formatted: Hypotheses and statistical analyses were pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/hd3yq">https://osf.io/hd3yq</ref>) repository.

text.text: Inclusion criteria for the eMotion study required that participants (a) were at least 18 years old, (b) were fluent in German, (c) were in a committed romantic relationship for a minimum of six months, (d) had both partners in the relationship be willing to participate, and (e) had at least one partner own an Android smartphone.
This latter requirement was a technical constraint of the mobile sensing procedure, meaning that the digitally traced data reported in this study are drawn exclusively from Android users.
From an initial pool of enrolled participants (N = 496), we first excluded individuals who did not consent to the study's mobile sensing procedure (N = 110).

Those for whom no smartphone trace data were available despite having consented, were further excluded (N = 44), resulting in an analytic sample of 342 participants with both digital trace and EMA data.

Although we pre-registered an exclusion criterion of less than 40% EMA completion to minimize the risk of systematic bias from missing data (e.g., due to client-or server-side errors or missed prompts), no participants met this criterion.
The final sample had a mean age of 32.9 years (SD = 10.7, range = 18-78), with 48.8% of participants identifying as women, 50% as men, and 1.2% as non-binary or did not report.
Most participants had completed secondary education or higher (87.7%), with 54.1% holding a university degree.
Participants were employed either full-time (39.2%) or part-time (41.5%) and had been in their romantic relationship for an average of 8.1 years (SD = 7.7, range = 6 months -49 years).
Following registration for the eMotion study, participants attended a briefing session conducted by trained recruiters, during which the study's purpose, procedures, and data use were explained.
Informed consent, including separate consent to the mobile sensing component, was obtained at this stage.

Recruiters then entered essential participant information (e.g., couple ID and study start date) into the administrative backend of formR (Arslan et al., 2020), which was used to automate the EMA procedure.
text.formatted: Recruiters then entered essential participant information (e.g., couple ID and study start date) into the administrative backend of formR <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Arslan et al., 2020)</ref>, which was used to automate the EMA procedure.

text.text: Over the following 10 days, participants received six EMA prompts per day, delivered between 09:30 and 21:30.

The first five prompts were randomly distributed across prespecified intervals throughout the day, with fixed gaps between intervals to accommodate a 30-minute survey access window and an estimated 10-minute completion time.
The sixth and final prompt of each day was sent at a fixed time (21:30), with a 60-minute window to open the survey and 10 minutes to complete it.
Prompts were randomized independently for each participant and each day.
Participants who consented to the mobile sensing component were instructed to install the movisensXS app (http://www.movisens.com/) on their Android smartphones during the briefing session.
text.formatted: Participants who consented to the mobile sensing component were instructed to install the movisensXS app (<ref type="url" target="http://www.movisens.com/">www.movisens.com</ref>) on their Android smartphones during the briefing session.

text.text: This app enabled continuous passive collection of digital trace data throughout the study period.
All EMA and mobile sensing data were securely stored on university-protected servers.

Ethical approval for the eMotion study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of the Faculty of Psychology and Sports Science at the University of Münster, under registration number 2021-81-AM.
Psychological well-being.
Psychological well-being was assessed through three wellbeing indicators.
First, perceived stress was measured once during the end of day EMA prompt using the Stress Overload Scale (SOS; Amirkhan, 2018).
The scale consisted of five items capturing the extent to which participants felt overwhelmed by daily demands or stressors (e.g., "to what extent did you feel overwhelmed by your duties today?").
Responses were given on a 7-point scale (1: "not at all"; 7: "very much"), and a mean score was calculated so that higher scores reflected higher perceived stress.

Next, participants reported the intensity of seven emotions at each EMA prompt: happiness, relaxation, sadness, irritation, worry, depression, and exhaustion (Brans et al., 2013; Sonnentag et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Next, participants reported the intensity of seven emotions at each EMA prompt: happiness, relaxation, sadness, irritation, worry, depression, and exhaustion <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brans et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Sonnentag et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Responses were also given on a 7point scale (1: "not at all"; 7: "very much"), with higher scores indicating greater intensity of the respective emotion.
Since perceived stress was assessed at the day level only, emotion ratings were similarly aggregated to the day level to ensure temporal alignment across all outcome measures.

From these items, daily positive affect was computed by averaging happiness and relaxation scores across all available prompts within a day, while daily negative affect was computed by averaging sadness, irritation, worry, depression, and exhaustion scores across prompts within the same day.
Smartphone use purposes were derived from passively collected app use data obtained with the movisensXS app.
A two-step categorization process was applied to translate raw app event logs into theoretically meaningful use purpose indicators.

In the first step, logged app use events were classified into one of 26 app categories defined by Schoedel and colleagues (2022), including, among others, communication, social media, news, entertainment-related categories (e.g., reading, gaming, etc.), and various instrumental categories (e.g., navigation, shopping, etc.).
text.formatted: In the first step, logged app use events were classified into one of 26 app categories defined by <ref type="bibr">Schoedel and colleagues (2022)</ref>, including, among others, communication, social media, news, entertainment-related categories (e.g., reading, gaming, etc.), and various instrumental categories (e.g., navigation, shopping, etc.).

text.text: In the second step, these app categories were mapped onto the smartphone use purposes examined in the present study (Table 1).
text.formatted: In the second step, these app categories were mapped onto the smartphone use purposes examined in the present study (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The internet category was excluded because browser-based activity can serve any of the five use purposes, and it was not possible to determine browsing activity based on the available event logs.

The settings and system app categories were also excluded, as their typical use cases (e.g., changing screen brightness, accessing a smartphone's home screen or list of apps) do not align with any of the defined use purposes (Parry & Toth, 2025).
text.formatted: The settings and system app categories were also excluded, as their typical use cases (e.g., changing screen brightness, accessing a smartphone's home screen or list of apps) do not align with any of the defined use purposes <ref type="bibr">(Parry & Toth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Passive social use Use of social media apps without active social engagement with others (Rozgonjuk & Elhai, 2021; Verduyn et al., 2022) Social media Facebook, Instagram, Jodel, Pinterest, Tellonym, TikTok, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), etc.
text.formatted: Passive social use Use of social media apps without active social engagement with others <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Rozgonjuk & Elhai, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verduyn et al., 2022)</ref> Social media Facebook, Instagram, Jodel, Pinterest, Tellonym, TikTok, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), etc.

text.text: News consumption Use of apps meant to keep one informed about specific topics of interest consumption.

However, since the movisensXS app event logs do not provide information about the specific mode of engagement within an app, a categorical distinction between active and passive social media use cannot be made from trace data alone.

We therefore assumed that individuals' use of social media apps is predominantly passive in nature, consistent with prior work highlighting that passive content consumption constitutes the majority of individuals' time spent on social media (Verduyn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: We therefore assumed that individuals' use of social media apps is predominantly passive in nature, consistent with prior work highlighting that passive content consumption constitutes the majority of individuals' time spent on social media <ref type="bibr">(Verduyn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A comparable issue applies to entertainment, which includes app categories that encompass both passive (e.g., visual entertainment, audio entertainment, reading) and more active forms of media engagement (e.g., gaming, creativity, photo editing).
While acknowledging this difference in engagement, we grouped these app types together since they share the common function of facilitating process-related gratification (van Deursen et al., 2015).
text.formatted: While acknowledging this difference in engagement, we grouped these app types together since they share the common function of facilitating process-related gratification <ref type="bibr">(van Deursen et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, regarding practical use, the spirituality app category was included on grounds that apps in this category (e.g., meditation guides, prayer apps) typically support structured daily routines and thus serve a broadly practical function in individuals' daily lives.
We acknowledge that this classification is debatable and have conducted a sensitivity analysis using data that excluded the spirituality app category from the mapping process.
The results of this sensitivity analysis did not meaningfully differ from our reported findings.
Following the categorization procedure, app use sessions were identified from screen on and screen off events recorded in the app event logs (Parry & Toth, 2025).
text.formatted: Following the categorization procedure, app use sessions were identified from screen on and screen off events recorded in the app event logs <ref type="bibr">(Parry & Toth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Sessions reflecting eight or more uninterrupted hours of screen time were considered implausible logging artifacts and excluded.

In the remaining sessions, app-specific use cases reflecting three hours of uninterrupted use or more (e.g., three or more uninterrupted hours on Bumble) were similarly considered implausible and excluded.
Our pre-processing script additionally flagged fourteen hour or longer gaps between use sessions, since they may similarly reflect logging errors.
However, no such gaps were found in our app log data.
Finally, daily use duration (in minutes) was calculated for each smartphone use purpose by summing app-level durations within each purpose category across each study day.

To ensure that notable associations between specific use purposes and well-being represent purpose-specific patterns, independent of participants' overall smartphone engagement, we included daily screen time as a covariate in all models (Pieh et al., 2025; Toh et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To ensure that notable associations between specific use purposes and well-being represent purpose-specific patterns, independent of participants' overall smartphone engagement, we included daily screen time as a covariate in all models <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Pieh et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Toh et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Daily screen time was computed as the total duration of all app use sessions per day, across all app categories.

The eMotion study dataset is dyadic in origin, meaning that observations from partners within the same couple may be statistically interdependent, partially violating the statistical assumptions underlying conventional individual-level analyses (Arican-Dinc & Gable, 2026; Pauw et al., 2024; Randall et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The eMotion study dataset is dyadic in origin, meaning that observations from partners within the same couple may be statistically interdependent, partially violating the statistical assumptions underlying conventional individual-level analyses <ref type="bibr">(Arican-Dinc & Gable, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Pauw et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Randall et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Among the 342 participants included in the present study, both partners provided trace data in 112 couples (N = 224 participants), while in 118 couples only one partner contributed trace data.
To address this dyadic interdependence and simultaneously provide an internal test of the robustness of our findings, we employed a dyadic random split procedure.
Partners from couples with complete trace data were randomly assigned to one of two subsets, thus separating dyad members across analytic samples.
Individuals from couples with only one participating partner were randomly assigned to either subset.
This procedure yielded two subsets (Subset A: n = 169; Subset B: n = 173) for analysis.

Our conclusions were based on the consistency of associations across both subsets: a finding was considered robust when associations were statistically significant in the same direction in both subsets, while findings that emerged in only one subset were treated as exploratory and interpreted with caution.

To test our hypotheses, we estimated a series of multilevel models using the package 'lme4' (Bates et al., 2015) in R (R Core Team, 2024), examining the associations between daily smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being outcomes.
text.formatted: To test our hypotheses, we estimated a series of multilevel models using the package 'lme4' <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref> in R (R Core Team, 2024), examining the associations between daily smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being outcomes.

text.text: Given the nested structure of our data, with daily observations nested within individuals, multilevel modeling was used to simultaneously estimate between-person and within-person associations.

Consistent with our previous study (Adiasto et al., 2026), for each outcome variable (positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress), separate models were estimated for each smartphone use purpose (active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, or practical use).
text.formatted: Consistent with our previous study <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>, for each outcome variable (positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress), separate models were estimated for each smartphone use purpose (active social use, passive social use, news consumption, entertainment, or practical use).

text.text: Each model included study day as a covariate and daily screen time as a control variable, representing participants' overall smartphone engagement.

To decompose between-and within-person effects, daily use duration for each use purpose was separated into a person-mean component (representing stable individual differences in typical use) and a person-mean-centered component (representing day-to-day deviations from individuals' typical use).

Days on which participants did not use their smartphone for a given purpose contributed a value of zero to the daily duration variable and were included in the computation of person-means and personmean-centered scores.
This approach ensured that estimates reflected associations across all observed days, including non-use days, rather than conditioning on days when a given purpose was engaged.
Random intercepts and random slopes were specified for the within-person effects of each smartphone use purpose to allow for individual variation in these associations.
In cases where models failed to converge with this initial structure, the random slopes were dropped, retaining random intercepts only.

We did not anticipate that these differences would meaningfully influence the associations between smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being, thus both subsets were retained for subsequent analyses.
Table 3 summarizes the pattern of associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being across both data subsets.

text.text: Across all models, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for positive affect, negative affect, and perceived stress ranged from .51 to .64, indicating that a meaningful proportion of variance in psychological well-being reflected stable differences between individuals.
Marginal R² values ranged from 0.6% to 9.2% across all models, suggesting that fixed effects explained a consistently small proportion of variance in psychological well-being.

Meanwhile, conditional R² values ranged from 53.2% to 65.8%, suggesting that a moderate proportion of variance in psychological well-being could be reliably attributed to the random effects structure of each estimated model.
Below, we report more detailed results organized by smartphone use purpose.
In each subsection, we first report between-person associations, followed by within-person associations, with findings from both subsets presented simultaneously for each use purpose.
Associations that were statistically significant in the same direction in both subsets were considered robust, while significant associations present in only one subset were treated as exploratory.
Additionally, we note the direction and approximate magnitude of non-significant associations when informative.
Between-person associations.
Participants with higher daily active social use reported lower positive affect in Subset A (β = -.20, p = .008) but not in Subset B (β = .09, p = .199).

Between-person associations between active social use and negative affect were not statistically significant in either subset (Subset A: β = .09, p = .168; Subset B: β = .06, p = .309), though both associations pointed towards higher negative affect among participants with higher daily active social use.
Lastly, between-person active social use was associated with higher perceived stress in Subset A (β = .42, p < .001) but not Subset B (β = .11, p = .287).
text.formatted: Lastly, between-person active social use was associated with higher perceived stress in Subset A (β = .42, p < .001) but not Subset B (β = .11, p = .287).

text.text: We note that the between-person stress association in Subset A is especially large in magnitude relative to other associations observed in this study.
However, its non-replication in Subset B warrants caution.
As none of the between-person associations above were statistically significant in the same direction across both subsets, they were treated as exploratory.
Within-person associations.
On days when participants engaged in more active social use than was typical for them, positive affect was lower in both Subset A (β = -.05, p = .032) and Subset B (β = -.04, p = .015).

Within-person associations with negative affect (Subset A: β = .03, p = .040; Subset B: β = .02, p = .211) and perceived stress (Subset A: β = .08, p = .018; Subset B: β = .04, p = .179) were statistically significant in Subset A but not Subset B. Both associations were directionally consistent across subsets, pointing towards higher negative affect and perceived stress on days of elevated active social use.
However, standardized estimates were noticeably smaller in Subset B and did not reach statistical significance.
As such, these associations were treated as indicative but not robust.

Participants with higher daily news consumption reported higher positive affect (β = .12, p = .037), lower negative affect (β = -.10, p = .023), and lower perceived stress (β = -.18, p = .044) in Subset A. Despite this, Subset B estimates for negative affect and perceived stress were directionally consistent with Subset A, pointing towards lower negative affect and stress among participants with higher daily news consumption.
As none of the above between-person associations were statistically significant in the same direction across subsets, they were treated as exploratory.
