We noted that statistically significant associations between smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being were most often present in Subset A. Given that Subset A contained a larger proportion of female participants than Subset B, we conducted a sensitivity analysis in which all multilevel models were re-estimated with the addition of gender as a control variable.

The results of this sensitivity analysis did meaningfully change the magnitude, direction, and statistical significance of the above reported associations between smartphone use purposes and well-being.
The present study investigated the between-and within-person associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being.
Across two independently analyzed subsets, our findings show that the emerging pattern was one of limited and largely inconsistent associations (see Table 3 for an overview).
text.formatted: Across two independently analyzed subsets, our findings show that the emerging pattern was one of limited and largely inconsistent associations (see Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref> for an overview).

text.text: The one consistent relationship across subsets was a within-person association between active social use and positive affect, suggesting that on days when participants used their phones for active social purposes more than was typical for them, they reported lower positive affect.

This complements prior studies reporting significant between-person associations between active social use and well-being, in which individuals who used chat apps more often reported lower well-being compared to those who used chat apps less (Chan, 2018; Rotondi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: This complements prior studies reporting significant between-person associations between active social use and well-being, in which individuals who used chat apps more often reported lower well-being compared to those who used chat apps less <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Chan, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Rotondi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Further, our finding supports the idea that smartphone-based communication may lead to lower feelings of social connectedness, and thus lower well-being (Kroencke et al., 2023; Waytz & Gray, 2018).
text.formatted: Further, our finding supports the idea that smartphone-based communication may lead to lower feelings of social connectedness, and thus lower well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Kroencke et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Waytz & Gray, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond this, most associations were either non-significant, directionally inconsistent across subsets, or significant in only one subset.
Notably, passive social use was not reliably associated with any psychological well-being outcome when measured with device logged data.

This contrasts much of the existing literature relying on self-reported measures, including our own self-report study, which position passive social use among the most consistent negative predictors of well-being (Adiasto et al., 2026; Meier & Krause, 2023; Verduyn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This contrasts much of the existing literature relying on self-reported measures, including our own self-report study, which position passive social use among the most consistent negative predictors of well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Meier & Krause, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verduyn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these results contribute to an increasingly cautious perspective within the literature, which argues that the effects of smartphone use are neither as pervasive nor as uniform as often portrayed (Johannes et al., 2021; Nawaz, 2024; Schenkel et al., 2025; Winbush et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Together, these results contribute to an increasingly cautious perspective within the literature, which argues that the effects of smartphone use are neither as pervasive nor as uniform as often portrayed <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Johannes et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Nawaz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Schenkel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Winbush et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Overall, our findings suggest that the psychological consequences of smartphone use appear to be small and inconsistent when measured with digital trace data.

A key aim of our study was to evaluate whether digitally traced smartphone use purposes provide a more informative account of the relationship between smartphone use and psychological well-being, particularly beyond aggregate measures such as screen time.
Our findings offer partial support for this proposition, but with important caveats depending on the level of analysis considered:

At the between-person level, our findings demonstrate that no associations between smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being were consistent (i.e., statistically significant in the same direction) across both subsets.
This means that individuals who differed in their degree of engagement with each use purpose did not systematically differ in well-being.

Despite this, we note that several indicative associations emerged in Subset A. First, based on our prior self-report study (Adiasto et al., 2026), we hypothesized that digitally traced active social use would be positive associated with positive affect and stress.
text.formatted: Despite this, we note that several indicative associations emerged in Subset A. First, based on our prior self-report study <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>, we hypothesized that digitally traced active social use would be positive associated with positive affect and stress.

text.text: However, contrary to what we expected, individuals with higher active social use reported lower positive affect and higher stress.

One possible explanation for this finding is that individuals with higher active social use may have inadvertently displaced activities that are greatly beneficial to well-being, such as face-to-face communication or sleep, which ultimately resulted in lower well-being overall (Castelo et al., 2025; Kushlev & Leitao, 2020).
text.formatted: One possible explanation for this finding is that individuals with higher active social use may have inadvertently displaced activities that are greatly beneficial to well-being, such as face-to-face communication or sleep, which ultimately resulted in lower well-being overall <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Castelo et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Kushlev & Leitao, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Next, we examined the role of digitally traced news consumption in an exploratory manner, and we found that individuals with higher news consumption reported more favorable outcomes across all three well-being measures.

While these between-person news consumption associations were not replicated in Subset B, we note that the directional patterns are consistent with prior work suggesting that informationseeking behavior may support content-related need fulfilment and well-being (Boukes & Vliegenthart, 2017; de Hoog & Verboon, 2020; Kelly & Sharot, 2021; Van Deursen et al., 2015), thus warranting further investigation in future studies with larger and more diverse samples.
text.formatted: While these between-person news consumption associations were not replicated in Subset B, we note that the directional patterns are consistent with prior work suggesting that informationseeking behavior may support content-related need fulfilment and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boukes & Vliegenthart, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">de Hoog & Verboon, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kelly & Sharot, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Van Deursen et al., 2015)</ref>, thus warranting further investigation in future studies with larger and more diverse samples.

text.text: The passive social use null findings were particularly striking.
We hypothesized that digitally traced passive social use would be associated with lower well-being.
However, not only was passive social use unassociated with psychological well-being in either subset, but several associations also reversed direction across subsets.
Overall, this pattern suggests that the between-person associations between passive social use and psychological well-being are, at best, negligible under digitally traced assessment.
This pattern contrasts markedly with our prior self-report study, in which passive social use was among the most consistent negative predictors of well-being (Adiasto et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This pattern contrasts markedly with our prior self-report study, in which passive social use was among the most consistent negative predictors of well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: One plausible explanation for this divergence is that self-reported passive social use may not only reflect actual scrolling behavior but also individuals' concerns about their social media use.

In our self-report study, this perceptual bias may have inflated the reported associations with well-being through shared method variance (Orben & Przybylski, 2019; Parry et al., 2021; Podsakoff et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In our self-report study, this perceptual bias may have inflated the reported associations with well-being through shared method variance <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Orben & Przybylski, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Parry et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Podsakoff et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When using digital trace data, which provides the opportunity to disentangle perceived use from actual use, this inflation is removed and the association attenuates accordingly.

This interpretation is consistent with the broader pattern of evidence in the current literature, which underscores how self-report studies tend to find more consistent and more pronounced associations between smartphone use and well-being (Johannes et al., 2021; Shaw et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with the broader pattern of evidence in the current literature, which underscores how self-report studies tend to find more consistent and more pronounced associations between smartphone use and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Johannes et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Shaw et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the within-person level, the pattern of findings was overall similarly limited.
We hypothesized that digitally traced active social use would be positively associated with stress (Adiasto et al., 2026), but our findings provided no support for this.
text.formatted: We hypothesized that digitally traced active social use would be positively associated with stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>, but our findings provided no support for this.

text.text: However, one association met our specified replication criterion: on days with higher than typical active social use, participants reported lower positive affect in both subsets.
This within-person association was small in magnitude, but directionally consistent and statistically significant across both independent samples.

The finding that active social use is associated with lower positive affect within individuals over time, while between-person associations between the two variables being inconsistent, is theoretically plausible.
By nature, active social smartphone use is responsive to the events of daily life.
Individuals reach for their phones to communicate when something happens, when they need support, or when they feel isolated (Bilston et al., 2026; Chan, 2018; Rotondi et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Individuals reach for their phones to communicate when something happens, when they need support, or when they feel isolated <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bilston et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Chan, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Rotondi et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As such, higher than typical active social use on a given day may reflect days with elevated interpersonal demands, conflict, or need for connection, which are circumstances that would independently predict lower positive affect (Shi et al., 2023).
text.formatted: As such, higher than typical active social use on a given day may reflect days with elevated interpersonal demands, conflict, or need for connection, which are circumstances that would independently predict lower positive affect <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Shi et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, the within-person association may partly reflect emotion-driven use rather than a direct causal effect of active social use on mood (Marciano et al., 2022).
text.formatted: From this perspective, the within-person association may partly reflect emotion-driven use rather than a direct causal effect of active social use on mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Marciano et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Disentangling these directions of influence would require longitudinal designs capable of modelling the temporal ordering of use and affect within days, which is an important direction for future research.

Further, it is important to consider the time scale at which the above associations were observed, as the day-level window that was the focus of this study may not have been appropriate for every use purpose and well-being outcome.

It is plausible that some use purposes are associated with well-being over relatively short intervals, for example when a received message, initiated conversation, or read news item shifts an individual's affect in a matter of minutes.
Other use purposes may instead operate cumulatively, becoming meaningful only when a pattern of use is sustained over weeks.
For example, the psychological mechanisms attributed to passive social use, such as upward social comparison, arguably belong to this broader time scale (Meier & Krause, 2023; Verduyn et al., 2022).
text.formatted: For example, the psychological mechanisms attributed to passive social use, such as upward social comparison, arguably belong to this broader time scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Meier & Krause, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Verduyn et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: A daily temporal window would thus be poorly suited to detect associations between passive social use and well-being.
A similar consideration may apply to other well-being outcomes.

Positive and negative affect may fluctuate substantially over the course of a single day, whereas perceived stress as assessed in the present study represented a summary appraisal of demands that may better respond to accumulated rather than momentary load (Verduyn et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Positive and negative affect may fluctuate substantially over the course of a single day, whereas perceived stress as assessed in the present study represented a summary appraisal of demands that may better respond to accumulated rather than momentary load <ref type="bibr">(Verduyn et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: As such, aggregating smartphone use purposes and psychological well-being at the day-level may have attenuated genuine, short-lived associations.

We acknowledge that this interpretation remains speculative given our data, but it points toward the value of studies that vary observation windows and examine both short-and longer-term associations within the same design (Klingelhoefer et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We acknowledge that this interpretation remains speculative given our data, but it points toward the value of studies that vary observation windows and examine both short-and longer-term associations within the same design <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Klingelhoefer et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study contributes to ongoing methodological discourse about how smartphone use should be measured (Ellis, 2019; Parry et al., 2021; Shaw et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The present study contributes to ongoing methodological discourse about how smartphone use should be measured <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Ellis, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Parry et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Shaw et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: By relying on passively collected digital trace data rather than self-reported estimates, the study avoids two key biases that inflate associations in self-report research, namely recall inaccuracy, which introduces random noise, and perceptual bias, where individuals' subjective sense of their smartphone use is itself associated with their well-being, independent of actual behavior (Sewall & Parry, 2021; Tkaczyk et al., 2024).
text.formatted: By relying on passively collected digital trace data rather than self-reported estimates, the study avoids two key biases that inflate associations in self-report research, namely recall inaccuracy, which introduces random noise, and perceptual bias, where individuals' subjective sense of their smartphone use is itself associated with their well-being, independent of actual behavior <ref type="bibr">(Sewall & Parry, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Tkaczyk et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, the associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and well-being were generally smaller, less consistent, and less directionally coherent than those observed in our prior self-report study, which was conducted using data from the same parent project (Adiasto et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In the present study, the associations between digitally traced smartphone use purposes and well-being were generally smaller, less consistent, and less directionally coherent than those observed in our prior self-report study, which was conducted using data from the same parent project <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adiasto et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In particular, the robust negative associations between passive social use and well-being that characterized the self-report findings were largely absent under objective measurement.

This converges with the broader pattern in the literature, where studies leveraging digital trace data consistently yield more modest associations than self-report studies (große Deters et al., 2026; Johannes et al., 2021; Shaw et al., 2020; Winbush et al., 2025), and provides support to the notion that self-report associations may be inflated by shared method variance and perceptual bias rather than reflecting genuine behavioral effects.
text.formatted: This converges with the broader pattern in the literature, where studies leveraging digital trace data consistently yield more modest associations than self-report studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(große Deters et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Johannes et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Shaw et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Winbush et al., 2025)</ref>, and provides support to the notion that self-report associations may be inflated by shared method variance and perceptual bias rather than reflecting genuine behavioral effects.

text.text: That said, the use of digital trace data also comes with its own set of limitations.
Multiple assumptions about individuals' typical patterns of smartphone use need to be made and fine-tuned to derive meaningful behavior proxies from raw app use data (Parry & Toth, 2025).
text.formatted: Multiple assumptions about individuals' typical patterns of smartphone use need to be made and fine-tuned to derive meaningful behavior proxies from raw app use data <ref type="bibr">(Parry & Toth, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The systematic categorization of different apps (Schoedel et al., 2022), and their subsequent functional categorization into use purposes in the present study, may reflect individual-or group-level biases among researchers.
text.formatted: The systematic categorization of different apps <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Schoedel et al., 2022)</ref>, and their subsequent functional categorization into use purposes in the present study, may reflect individual-or group-level biases among researchers.

text.text: Crucially, different ethical and technical considerations may limit the extent to which individuals' true smartphone use behavior can be captured by digital trace data.

For example, passive sensing of an individual's actual activity within specific apps is difficult from an ethical standpoint, but this information is necessary to accurately determine whether specific interactions with an app were active (e.g., sending a direct message on Instagram) or passive (e.g., scrolling through one's Instagram feed) in nature.
In such cases, self-reported data may still provide a meaningful way to gain insight about individuals' actual, momentary experiences with their smartphones.

Relatedly, in several models, the associations between screen time and well-being outcomes were statistically significant in Subset A but not Subset B, mirroring the inconsistency observed for use purpose associations (see Tables S1-S5).
text.formatted: Relatedly, in several models, the associations between screen time and well-being outcomes were statistically significant in Subset A but not Subset B, mirroring the inconsistency observed for use purpose associations (see Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1-S5</ref>).

text.text: Past studies have proposed that the inconsistent associations between smartphone use and well-being in current literature are a product of ignoring the heterogeneity inherent to individuals' smartphone use behavior (Griffioen et al., 2021; Nawaz, 2024; Schenkel et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Past studies have proposed that the inconsistent associations between smartphone use and well-being in current literature are a product of ignoring the heterogeneity inherent to individuals' smartphone use behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Griffioen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Nawaz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Schenkel et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Zhao et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The limited pattern of associations we found for both screen time and smartphone use purposes suggests that the way smartphone use is measured appears to be a more fundamental source of inconsistency than the level of aggregation at which smartphone use is assessed.
A central contribution of this study is its simultaneous examination of between-person and within-person associations.

The divergence between these two levels, where the only robust finding was an association at the within-person level, has important implications for how associations between smartphone use and psychological well-being should be studied and interpreted.
Between-person associations indicate whether individuals who typically use their smartphones more for a given purpose tend to report higher or lower well-being on average.

Such associations are susceptible to confounding by stable individual characteristics, including personality, social circumstances, and occupational demands, which may simultaneously predict both smartphone use behavior and well-being (Anglim et al., 2020; Beierle et al., 2020; Nogueira & Sequeira, 2024).
text.formatted: Such associations are susceptible to confounding by stable individual characteristics, including personality, social circumstances, and occupational demands, which may simultaneously predict both smartphone use behavior and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anglim et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Beierle et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Nogueira & Sequeira, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, the absence of robust between-person associations in the present study does not imply that smartphone use purposes are irrelevant to well-being.
Rather, it suggests that stable differences in use are not independently associated with stable differences in well-being after accounting for overall smartphone engagement.

By contrast, within-person associations hold the individual constant and capture whether changes in an individual's own use behavior on a given day correspond to changes in their well-being on the same day.

The robust within-person association between active social use and positive affect is therefore more directly informative about the psychological consequences of actual variation in use behavior, though it remains observational and cannot establish direction of causality.

The divergence between levels observed in our study parallels findings from other intensive longitudinal studies of digital behavior and well-being, which have similarly noted that between-person and within-person associations do not always converge (große Deters & Schoedel, 2024; Marciano et al., 2022).
text.formatted: The divergence between levels observed in our study parallels findings from other intensive longitudinal studies of digital behavior and well-being, which have similarly noted that between-person and within-person associations do not always converge <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(große Deters & Schoedel, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Marciano et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Several features of the present work merit a brief commentary, as they influence how our findings should be weighed.
The present study distinguished between functionally distinct use purposes rather than treating smartphone use as a single aggregate.
These use purposes were derived from device logged data instead of self-reports, and estimated associations were obtained at both the between-and within-person levels.

Notably, the dyadic random split procedure addressed interdependence among partners while providing an internal robustness check, such that each association was evaluated against two samples rather than one.
Consistency across subsets is a relatively more demanding criterion than statistical significance in a single sample, and in the present work only one association met it.
Since each subset comprised roughly half the available participants, non-replication across subsets may either reflect lower statistical power or genuine instability in observed associations.
These two possibilities cannot be distinguished given our data.
Despite this, associations that emerged consistently across subsets rest on firmer ground than those that appeared in one, and reporting the two subsets separately makes that distinction visible.

Since much of the literature on smartphone use and well-being rests on single-sample findings of comparable magnitude (Meier & Reinecke, 2021; Vahedi & Saiphoo, 2018), we encourage future studies to build internal replication checks of this kind into their design.
text.formatted: Since much of the literature on smartphone use and well-being rests on single-sample findings of comparable magnitude <ref type="bibr">(Meier & Reinecke, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Vahedi & Saiphoo, 2018)</ref>, we encourage future studies to build internal replication checks of this kind into their design.

text.text: Several limitations should then be considered when interpreting the present findings:
First, the study's sample was recruited from a coupled population in Germany, with sensing data available exclusively from Android users.
These characteristics may limit the generalizability of the findings to single individuals, users of other operating systems, and different cultural context.
Future studies would thus benefit from more diverse and representative samples.
Second, the two-step categorization of smartphone use purposes from raw app event log data involved several simplifying assumptions.
Most notably, all social media app use was classified as passive social use, despite social media apps supporting both active and passive engagement.
The app event logs in the present study do not permit differentiation between modes of engagement within an app.
Consequently, this assumption cannot be relaxed with the available data.
Similarly, the entertainment category encompasses both passive (e.g., streaming) and more active (e.g., gaming) forms of engagement, which may have distinct psychological consequences.
Future work using more granular sensing approaches, for example, through integration of notification data or interaction logs, may allow for finergrained distinctions within these categories.
Additionally, internet browser app use was excluded from the categorization due to the inability to classify browsing sessions by purpose.
Future studies should consider how to handle this category, particularly given the potential volume of browsing activity it may represent.

Third, the present study focused on the duration of smartphone use purposes but did not capture the content consumed, the social context of use, or individuals' motivations for engaging in a given activity.
These contextual factors are likely to moderate the associations between use purposes and well-being.
For example, the psychological impact of news consumption is known to depend on the valence and personal relevance of the content (Boukes & Vliegenthart, 2017; de Hoog & Verboon, 2020).
text.formatted: For example, the psychological impact of news consumption is known to depend on the valence and personal relevance of the content <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Boukes & Vliegenthart, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">de Hoog & Verboon, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies could thus implement ways to assess the type of content individuals view on the different news apps they use.
Finally, the observational nature of the study precludes causal inference.
The withinperson association between active social use and positive affect may reflect reverse causality.

It remains possible that in situations individuals with lower psychological well-being individuals selectively engage in certain smartphone activities rather than these activities directly influencing well-being.

For instance, the observed within-person association between active social use and positive affect may reflect individuals turning to social communication as a form of emotion regulation when experiencing lower mood.

Such reciprocal dynamics remain understudied (Elmer et al., 2025; Marciano et al., 2022) and could be addressed in future work through experimental or quasi-experimental designs, or through longitudinal analytical approaches such as random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; Mulder & Hamaker, 2021).
text.formatted: Such reciprocal dynamics remain understudied <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Elmer et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Marciano et al., 2022)</ref> and could be addressed in future work through experimental or quasi-experimental designs, or through longitudinal analytical approaches such as random-intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Mulder & Hamaker, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The present study examined whether digitally traced smartphone use purposes were associated with psychological well-being, using passively collected app use data from a large ecological momentary assessment study.
Across two analytic subsets, one robust finding emerged: on days of higher than typical active social smartphone use, individuals reported lower positive affect.

Beyond this, associations between digitally traced use purposes and wellbeing were small, inconsistent across subsets, and largely absent for purposes that have been more consistently implicated in self-report studies.

These findings suggest that the psychological consequences of actual smartphone use behavior, as opposed to perceived or self-reported use, are more limited and more context-dependent than typically portrayed.
